en: The Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...

There was a great assembly of thirty-two thousand bhikṣus, along with seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—renowned throughout the world, who had attained dhāraṇīs, achieved eloquence and inexhaustible joy in preaching, dwelt unmovingly in samādhi, were well-able to comprehend inexhaustible wisdom, had attained profound dharma-patience and entered deep dharma-gates;

who, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, had fully accomplished all the wholesome dharmas they cultivated, subdued all māras and defeated all enemies, had taken hold of the most honored and pure buddha-fields, and possessed great compassion with their bodies adorned by the various marks.

They have reached the further shore through great vigor; they are skilled in all expedient means of speech; their conduct and deportment are fully pure; they have all attained abiding in the three gates of liberation; they penetrate the three periods of time with unimpeded wisdom; they have resolved their minds never to abandon anything; they possess the power of mindfulness regarding the meaning of the teachings, as well as patience and wisdom.

The virtues of these bodhisattvas are all such as these—their names are: Bodhisattva Turning the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma, Bodhisattva Turning the Wheel of Dharma upon Resolving the Mind, Bodhisattva Unimpeded Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, Bodhisattva Stainless Purity, Bodhisattva Removing All Obscurations, and Bodhisattva Manifesting Pure Deportment.
The Bodhisattva Whose Appearance is Loved by All, the Bodhisattva King of Majestic Features and Pure Intent, the Bodhisattva Who Deceives No Sentient Being,
the Bodhisattva Ocean of Immeasurable Merit and Intent, the Bodhisattva Whose Faculties are Constantly Settled and Undisturbed,
the Bodhisattva True Sound, the Bodhisattva Praised by All Devas, and the Dhāraṇī.
The Bodhisattva Sovereign King, the Bodhisattva Adorned with Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince,
the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Sumeru Peak King, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Adorned Pure Mind of Oceanic Virtues,
the Bodhisattva Great Purity, the Bodhisattva Great Mark, and the Bodhisattva Radiant Mark.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Prabhāśrī, Viśuddhamati, Nandirāja, Dṛḍhavīrya, and Dṛḍhamati— these and seventy-two thousand other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas—

as well as all the Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas of the trichiliocosm, together with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who were well-known to the masses, who had planted various roots of goodness, and who delighted in the Great Dharma, all came to this assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind (Dṛḍhamati), while in the great assembly, had this thought: "I shall now question the Tathāgata.

By means of these questions, I wish to protect the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Saṃgha; to cause the palaces of the Māras to be hidden and obscured; to subdue those who possess excessive pride; to cause those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them now; to cause those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase them; to cause those who have not yet resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to resolve their minds upon it; to cause those who have already resolved their minds to become non-retrogressive; and to cause those who are already non-retrogressive to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

For those who calculate that there is something to be attained and who abide in various views, he causes them all to give rise to the mind of renunciation; for those who delight in the Lesser Dharma, he causes them not to doubt the Great Dharma; and for those who delight in the Great Dharma, he causes them to give rise to joy.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“I now wish to ask a few questions regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha said to Resolute Mind:
“Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you so as to bring you joy.”
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Is there a samādhi that can cause a bodhisattva to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, always remaining inseparable from the meeting and beholding of all Buddhas, able to universally illumine the ten directions with light, and obtain sovereign wisdom to destroy all Māras?”
They attain sovereign wisdom and obtain spontaneous wisdom;
they attain the wisdom of non-arising and are thus able not to follow others;
they attain uninterrupted eloquence that extends to the end of the future.
Having attained the bases of psychic power, he receives immeasurable life.

To those who delight in the Śrāvaka vehicle, he shows the Śrāvaka vehicle; to those who delight in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he shows the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and to those who delight in the Mahāyāna, he reveals the Mahāyāna for them.

They thoroughly penetrate the teachings of the śrāvakas yet do not enter the path of the śrāvakas; they thoroughly penetrate the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas yet do not enter the path of the pratyekabuddhas; they thoroughly penetrate the teachings of the Buddhas yet do not undergo ultimate extinction.
They manifest the physical form and deportment of śrāvakas, yet inwardly they do not depart from the bodhicitta of the Buddha;
they manifest the physical form and deportment of pratyekabuddhas, yet inwardly they do not depart from the great compassion of the Buddha.
By the power of the illusion-like samādhi, they manifest the physical form, color, and majestic deportment of a Tathāgata;

by the power of roots of goodness, they manifest dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, receiving their final birth, entering the womb, being born, leaving home, and sitting at the site of enlightenment; by the power of profound wisdom, they manifest turning the wheel of Dharma; by the power of skillful means, they manifest entering nirvana; by the power of samādhi, they manifest the distribution of relics; and by the power of original vows, they manifest the extinction of the Dharma.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
What samādhi must be practiced to enable a bodhisattva to manifest such meritorious deeds while not ultimately entering into parinirvāṇa?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Dṛḍhamati! You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning as this.

You should know that you are capable of bringing great benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings; out of compassion for the world, you will bring profit, peace, and security to devas and humans, benefiting bodhisattvas in both this life and future lives.

You should know that you have already deeply planted roots of goodness, having made offerings to and drawn near countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in the past; you have traversed all paths to subdue demonic adversaries;

you have attained sovereign wisdom within the Buddha-dharma to teach, transform, and protect the assembly of Bodhisattvas; you have already mastered the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, and have achieved mastery in question-and-answer discourse before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Resolute Mind!

Within this assembly, the Tathāgata does not see any among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, nor any śrāvakas or those seeking pratyekabuddhahood, who would be able to ask such a question; only you, O Greatly Adorned Ones, are capable of initiating such an inquiry."
Listen attentively now, and reflect upon it well!
I shall explain for you how the various bodhisattvas achieve samādhi, whereby they attain merits even greater than this.
Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said to Dṛḍhamati:

“There is a samādhi named Śūraṅgama. If there are bodhisattvas who attain this samādhi, they can manifest parinirvāṇa as you have asked, yet they do not undergo ultimate extinction; they manifest various forms and colors, yet they do not destroy the characteristics of form;
they travel everywhere through all buddha-lands, yet they make no conceptual distinctions regarding those lands;
and they are able to encounter all buddhas, yet they do not differentiate them from the nature of equality.”
He manifests the universal practice of all conditioned activities, yet is able to thoroughly know the purity of all such activities;
he is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans, yet remains free from self-exaltation, arrogance, and heedlessness;
he displays the sovereign power of all Māras, yet does not rely upon or adhere to the deeds of Māra.
They pervade all within the three realms of existence, yet remain unmoved by the characteristics of phenomena;
they manifest birth throughout all realms of rebirth, yet do not discriminate between the characteristics of those realms;
they are skillfully able to explain all dharma-terms, revealing their meanings through various expressions, while knowing that letters enter into the state of equality.
They make no conceptual distinctions regarding any forms of speech; they constantly abide in meditative concentration while manifesting transformations to guide sentient beings;
they practice the patience of exhaustion and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, yet speak of all phenomena as having the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
they walk alone without fear, like lions.
At that time, all the great assemblies in the gathering—the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Heavenly Kings—all had this thought:
"We have never yet even heard the name of this samādhi, much less heard its meaning explained."
It is a great gain and a source of true benefit that we have now come to see the Buddha and have all together heard the name of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi being spoken.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who seeks the path of the Buddha hears the meaning and intent of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and believes and understands it without doubt, you should know that such a person will certainly never again regress from the path of the Buddha; how much more so for one who, having believed, receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains it to others, and practices according to its teaching?
At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings all had this thought:

"We shall now, for the sake of the Buddha Tathāgata, prepare a lion throne, a throne of the True Dharma, a throne of the Great Superior Being, a throne of great adornment, and a throne for turning the Great Wheel of Dharma; we shall cause the Tathāgata to preach the Śūraṅgama Samādhi upon this throne of ours."
Among them, each person thought to themselves:
"Only I have prepared the lion throne for the Buddha; no one else has been able to do so.
At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings—

For each Tathāgata, they prepared lion thrones—adorned, pure, majestic, lofty, and prominent—with immeasurable precious robes spread upon them, and all were provided with various wonderful jeweled canopies.

Furthermore, they fashioned railings out of various jewels; to the left and right of the thrones stood immeasurable jewel trees, their branches and leaves interlacing in symmetrical rows. Banners and streamers hung down, great jeweled curtains were unfurled, various jewels were intertwined as lattices, and precious bells were suspended, while a profusion of exquisite mixed flowers was scattered over them.

Various celestial incenses were burned to perfume the air, and the radiance of gold, silver, and myriad jewels intermingled in a dazzling array; every kind of adornment and purity was present without exception.
In an instant, before the Tathāgata, there appeared eighty-four thousand billion nayutas of precious lion thrones, all of which occupied the assembly without causing any obstruction.
Each of the sons of heaven did not see the other seats, and each thought to themselves:
"I alone have prepared this lion throne for the Buddha; the Buddha shall preach the Śūraṅgama Samādhi upon the seat I have prepared."
When the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Heavenly Kings had finished arranging their seats, they each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will sit upon our seats and preach the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."

Immediately, the World-Honored One manifested great supernatural power, sitting upon all eighty-four trillion nayutas of lion thrones; each of the devas saw the Buddha seated upon the very seat they had spread out for him, and could see no other seats.
A certain Śakra said to another Śakra,
"Behold the Tathāgata seated upon my throne.
In this manner, the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Heavenly Kings each spoke to one another.
"Behold the Tathāgata sitting upon my seat.
A certain Śākya said:
"The Tathāgata is now sitting only upon my seat, not upon yours."

At that time, because the Tathāgata was to deliver the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Heavenly Kings through their past karmic conditions, and furthermore, wishing to manifest slightly the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, as well as to bring the practices of the Mahāyāna to fulfillment, he caused the entire assembly to see the Tathāgata pervading eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* precious lion thrones.
The entire assembly was filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence; each rose from their seat, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha, and all spoke these words:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
With immeasurable majestic power, he causes each of the sons of the gods to fulfill their respective wishes.

Those sons of the gods who had prepared seats for the Tathāgata, upon witnessing the Buddha’s spiritual power, all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata, to eliminate the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings, and to protect the true Dharma so as not to sever the lineage of the Buddhas, we have all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“May we, in future ages, attain such majestic spiritual power as a Buddha, manifesting transformations just as the Tathāgata has done here and now.
At that time, the Buddha praised the sons of the gods, saying: “Excellent!”
Excellent! As you have said, to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings is the foremost offering to the Tathāgata.
At that time, among the assembly of Brahmās, there was a Brahmā King named Samacārin who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Which Tathāgata is the true one?”
“Is it upon my seat, or upon the other seats? The Buddha told Samacārin: “All dharmas are empty and like illusions;

they exist through combination, yet there is no creator. They all arise from conceptualization and discrimination; because they have no master, they emerge according to one’s own mind. These Tathāgatas are all truly real.”
What is meant by "reality"?
These Tathāgatas are fundamentally unborn from the beginning; therefore, they are real.
These Tathāgatas will likewise not exist hereafter; therefore, they are real.
These Tathāgatas are not comprised within the four great elements; therefore, they are real.
They are not comprised within the aggregates, sense-bases, or elements; therefore, they are real.
These Tathāgatas are equal and without distinction throughout the beginning, middle, and end; therefore, they are real.
“Brahmā King! These Tathāgatas are equal and without distinction. Why is this so?
These Tathāgatas are equal because the suchness of form is equal; they are equal because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is equal.

For this reason, they are equal. These Tathāgatas are equal because the suchness of the past is equal; they are equal because the suchness of the future is equal; they are equal because the suchness of the present is equal; they are equal because all phenomena are like illusions; they are equal because all phenomena are like reflections; they are equal because all phenomena are non-existent; and they are equal because there is no place from which they come and no place to which they go. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "Equal."
Just as all phenomena are equal, so too are these Tathāgatas!
Just as all sentient beings are equal, so too are these Tathāgatas!
Just as all those Buddhas in the world, so too are these Tathāgatas!
Just as all those worlds, so too are these Tathāgatas!
Therefore, all Buddhas are called "equal. Brahmā King!
Because these Tathāgatas do not transcend the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, they are called "equal."
Brahmā, you should know that the Tathāgata fully knows all dharmas to be thus equal; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be "equal" with respect to all dharmas.
The Brahma King Samacārin addressed the Buddha,
saying: "It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!"
"Having attained these dharmas of equality, the Tathāgata manifests to sentient beings by means of a body of wondrous form.
The Buddha said, "Brahmā King!
All of this is brought about by the power of the fundamental practices of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
For this reason, after the Tathāgata has attained these dharmas of equality, he manifests to sentient beings with a body of wondrous form.
When this Dharma was being taught, the Brahma King Samacārin and ten thousand Brahmās attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*) regarding all dharmas.
At that time, the Tathāgata withdrew his supernormal power; the various Buddhas and their seats no longer appeared, and the entire assembly saw only a single Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind:

"The Śūraṅgama Samādhi cannot be attained by bodhisattvas of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth stage; only a bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage can attain this Śūraṅgama Samādhi."
What is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
It is said:
cultivating and purifying the mind so that it is like empty space. First.
Second, observing the various minds of present sentient beings;
third, discerning the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings;
fourth, definitively knowing the causes and effects of sentient beings.
5. Among all karmas, knowing that there is no retribution for karma;
6. entering into various inclinations and, having entered them, not forgetting them;
7. directly knowing the immeasurable and diverse natures.

8. They are constantly able to sport in the Samādhi of Flower-like Sounds and can manifest to sentient beings the Samādhi of the Vajra Mind, attaining mastery over all meditative concentrations according to their will.
9. They universally observe all the various paths to which they go.
10. Attaining unimpeded knowledge of past lives;
11. Unobstructed divine vision; 12.
Attaining the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, yet not realizing it prematurely.
13. Attaining the wisdom of equal entry into the realms of form and formlessness;
14. Manifesting and sporting within all forms;
15. Knowing that all sounds are like the nature of an echo.
16. To enter into mindfulness and wisdom in accordance with the truth;
17. To gladden sentient beings with virtuous speech;
18. To preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
19. Knowing the proper time and the improper time;
20. Being able to transform the faculties;
21. Teaching the Dharma without falsehood.
Twenty-second: they enter the limit of reality in accordance with it;
twenty-third: they are well able to subdue and convert all classes of sentient beings;
twenty-fourth: they are fully capable of perfecting all the pāramitās.
Twenty-fifth, their deportment and movements have never differed from the norm.
Twenty-sixth, they destroy all recollections and false conceptualizations.
Twenty-seventh, they do not disrupt the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and exhaust its ultimate limit.
28. At one time manifesting their bodies so as to dwell in the presence of all Buddhas;
29. Able to uphold all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas;
30. Universally throughout all worlds, freely transforming their bodies like the appearance of reflections.
31. Skillfully expounding the various vehicles to deliver sentient beings, they are always able to protect and uphold the Triple Gem so that it is never interrupted.
32. They give rise to great adornment until the end of the future, yet their minds never harbor thoughts of weariness or exhaustion.
33. Everywhere in all places of birth, he is always able to manifest his body at the appropriate time without interruption.
34. In all places of birth, he manifests the performance of various deeds.
35. He is well able to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment.
36. He is well able to discern and know all sentient beings.
37. All those of the two vehicles cannot fathom him.
38. He is well able to fully know all categories of sounds. 39.
He can cause all dharmas to blaze forth with intensity.
40. He can cause one kalpa to become an asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
41. He can cause an asaṃkhyeya kalpa to become a single kalpa. 42.
He can cause a single country to enter into an asaṃkhyeya number of countries. 43.
He can cause an asaṃkhyeya number of countries to enter into a single country.
44. Entering immeasurable Buddha-lands into a single pore; 45.
Manifesting all sentient beings as entering into a single body; 46.
Realizing that all Buddha-lands are identical to empty space.
47. The body is able to reach all Buddha-lands without exception. 48.
All bodies are made to enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) so that they become bodiless.
49. One thoroughly penetrates the signlessness (animitta) of all dharmatās.
50. Being well able to comprehend all skillful means;
51. Being able to thoroughly penetrate the nature of all phenomena through what is spoken in a single sound;
52. Being able to expound a single phrase for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
53. Skillfully observing the distinctions among all dharma-gates; 54.
Skillfully knowing how to teach the Dharma through its similarities and differences, as well as in brief and detailed forms;
55. Skillfully knowing how to transcend all paths of Māra.
56. Emitting the great light of skillful means and wisdom.
57. Having wisdom as the foremost of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
58. The supernormal power of non-action is constantly present before him.
59. By means of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, they are able to cause all sentient beings to rejoice.
60. They manifest supernormal powers that penetrate the nature of all dharmas.
61. They are able to universally gather in all sentient beings through the methods of integration.
Sixty-two: Understanding the sixty-two types of languages of sentient beings throughout all worlds.
Sixty-three: Having no doubts regarding phenomena that are like illusions.
Sixty-four: Being able to exercise universal mastery over all places of birth.
65. Whatever things are required are provided according to one's wishes without lack. 66.
He manifests himself freely before all sentient beings. 67.
To both the virtuous and the non-virtuous, he is equally a field of merit.
68. Attaining entry into all the secret dharmas of the bodhisattvas;
69. Constantly emitting light that illuminates all worlds without exception;
70. Possessing wisdom so profound and far-reaching that none can fathom it.
His mind is like earth, water, fire, and wind (71).
He is skilled in the chapters, verses, and terminology of all dharmas, and thus turns the wheel of Dharma (72).
He is without obstruction regarding the stage of the Tathāgata (73).
Seventy-fourth: Spontaneously attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Seventy-fifth: Attaining the mind of suchness, which cannot be defiled by the stains of any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Seventy-sixth: Causing all waters to enter into a single pore without disturbing the nature of water.
Seventy-seventh: Cultivating and accumulating immeasurable roots of merit and virtue.
Seventy-eighth: Skillfully knowing all expedient means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Seventy-ninth: Being skillful in transformation, universally practicing all bodhisattva deeds.
80. The Buddha’s mind attains peace and stability regarding all dharmas.
81. Having attained the relinquishment of his former karma and physical body. 82.
He is able to enter the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
83. Manifesting the playful enjoyment of all desires at will; 84.
Hearing immeasurable teachings and being fully able to retain them; 85.
Seeking all dharmas with a mind that never tires.
86. He conforms to all worldly dharmas yet remains undefiled. 87.
Although he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas, he causes them all to perceive it as being like the time from morning until the midday meal.
88. He manifests various forms of physical infirmity—such as being crippled, maimed, lame, deaf, blind, or mute—to transform sentient beings.
89. One hundred thousand *guhyapada* vajra-wielding heroes constantly follow, protect, and attend upon him.
90. They are naturally able to contemplate and know the path of all Buddhas. 91.
They are able, in a single thought-moment, to manifest the reception of immeasurable and incalculable kalpas of lifespan. 92.
They manifest the practice of all the rituals and laws of the two vehicles, yet inwardly they do not abandon the practices of all Bodhisattvas.
93. Their minds are well-pacified, empty, and signless. 94.
While manifesting their own enjoyment among various musical performances, they do not inwardly abandon the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
Whether seen, heard, touched, or lived with, they are all able to bring immeasurable sentient beings to fulfillment (95).
They can manifest the path to Buddhahood in every thought-moment, leading those to be transformed according to their original capacities to attain liberation (96).
97. Manifesting entry into the womb and initial birth;
98. Renouncing the world and accomplishing the Buddha-way;
99. Turning the wheel of Dharma.
“Entering great parinirvāṇa yet not being extinguished forever” is the one hundredth. “Firm Mind!
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is thus immeasurable; it can fully manifest all the spiritual powers of a Buddha, so that immeasurable sentient beings all obtain benefit.”

Dṛḍhamati! The Śūraṅgama Samādhi cannot be known through a single matter, a single condition, or a single principle; all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, supernormal powers, and unimpeded wisdom are entirely contained within the Śūraṅgama.

Just as all streams—whether from ponds, springs, rivers, or mountain torrents—flow into the great ocean, so too do all the meditative concentrations of a bodhisattva reside within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
For example, a Wheel-Turning Sage King has great heroic generals, and all fourfold armies follow them.
Resolute Mind!

In the same way, all these dharma-gates—the gates of samādhi, the gates of meditative concentration, the gates of eloquence, the gates of liberation, the gates of dhāraṇī, the gates of supernormal power, and the gates of clear liberation—are entirely subsumed within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Whenever a bodhisattva practices the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all samādhis follow along.
Dṛḍhamati! Just as when a wheel-turning sage-king travels, the seven treasures all follow him;
so it is, Dṛḍhamati!
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is followed by all the factors that assist toward enlightenment; for this reason, this samādhi is named Śūraṅgama.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:

“When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he practices giving without seeking wealth. He freely bestows all such things as treasures, food and drink, clothing, elephants, horses, and carriages—whatever exists within the great trichiliocosm, the various great oceans, celestial palaces, and the human realm. All of this is brought about by his original merit, let alone what is accomplished at will through his supernormal powers.”
"This is called the fundamental cause, fruit, and retribution of the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi regarding the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
The Buddha told Resolute Mind (Dṛḍhamati):

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they no longer receive the precepts, yet they remain unshakable in their observance of them. For the sake of transforming and guiding all sentient beings, they manifest the practice of upholding the precepts and performing various dignified conducts; they demonstrate the commissioning of offenses and the subsequent eradication of faults and transgressions, while remaining inwardly pure and forever free from deficiency."

For the sake of transforming and teaching all sentient beings, he is born in the desire realm as a wheel-turning monarch, surrounded by a respectful retinue of court ladies. Although he appears to have a wife and children and indulges freely in the five desires, he remains constantly within meditative concentration and pure precepts, skillfully perceiving the faults and afflictions of the three realms of existence.
“Dṛḍhamati! This is called the fruit of retribution for the original practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Buddha told Dṛḍhamati:

“When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they practice patience because it is ultimately exhaustive: they practice patience because sentient beings do not arise; they practice patience because all dharmas do not originate; they practice patience because the mind has no form or color; they practice patience because they do not apprehend self or other; they practice patience because they do not dwell on birth and death; they practice patience by means of the nature of nirvāṇa; and they practice patience without destroying the dharma-nature.”
When a bodhisattva practices patience in this way, there is neither practice nor non-practice.
To transform sentient beings, they are born in the desire realm; they manifest anger and resentment while remaining inwardly pure.

They manifest the practice of detachment yet have no distance between themselves and others. To purify sentient beings, they violate worldly decorum, yet they never violate the nature of all phenomena.
There is currently that which is endured, yet there is no dharma; it is eternally settled and indestructible, such that it can be endured.

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience, they do so to sever the many hateful and evil minds of sentient beings, and thus constantly praise the merit of patience; furthermore, they neither grasp at anger nor grasp at patience.
"Resolute Mind!
This is called the fruit of the original practice and the retribution for the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:

"When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they exert great diligence to attain all wholesome dharmas, yet they do not stir the karma of body, speech, or mind. For the sake of those who are indolent, they manifest the practice of diligence, desiring to cause sentient beings to follow their example and learn from them, while remaining without any arousal or reception regarding all dharmas."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva fully knows that all phenomena (dharmas) eternally abide in the nature of reality (dharmatā), neither coming nor going; thus, while remaining far removed from the activities of body, speech, and mind, he is able to manifest the practice of vigor, yet he does not perceive any phenomenon that is accomplished.
They manifest the exertion of diligence within the world, yet remain without activity regarding either the internal or the external;
they are constantly able to travel to and from immeasurable Buddha-lands, yet their physical forms remain equal and unmoving;
they manifest the practice of all wholesome dharmas, yet they do not perceive good or evil within any phenomena.
He manifests the seeking of the Dharma and receiving instruction from others, yet regarding the Buddha-way he does not follow the teachings of another;
he manifests close attendance upon preceptors and teachers, yet he is the Honored One among all devas and humans;
he manifests diligent inquiry, yet within himself he has attained unimpeded eloquence.
Manifesting reverent conduct, they are venerated and looked up to by all devas and humans;
manifesting entry into the womb, they remain unstained by any phenomena;
manifesting birth, they perceive no arising or ceasing in any phenomena.
He manifests as a small child, yet his body and all his faculties are fully complete;
he manifests the practice of arts, medicine, incantations, literature, mathematics, and technical crafts, yet within he has long since attained mastery of them all;
he manifests the suffering of illness, yet he is eternally free from the afflictions of all defilements.
He manifests aging, yet his faculties have never been impaired from the beginning;
he manifests death, yet he has never experienced birth, cessation, or decline.
Resolute Mind!
"This is called the fruit of the original practice of the perfection of vigor for a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:

"Although a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi knows that all dharmas are eternally of a fixed nature, he nevertheless demonstrates to sentient beings the distinctions among the various dhyānas."
Manifesting a body that dwells in dhyāna to transform those with distracted minds, yet perceiving no distraction within all phenomena;
seeing all phenomena as having the characteristics of the *dharmatā*, they tame the mind so it remains unmoving in dhyāna;
manifesting various modes of deportment—coming, going, sitting, and reclining—yet remaining eternally tranquil within meditative concentration.
He manifests speech and discourse just like that of ordinary people, yet he never abandons the marks of various meditative concentrations;
out of compassion for sentient beings, he enters cities, villages, and provinces, yet he remains constantly in samādhi;
and for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he manifests the act of eating, yet he remains constantly in samādhi.

His body is as firm and solid as a diamond; it is internally substantial and not hollow, being indestructible. Within it there are no receptacles for undigested food, nor for digested food, nor excrement or urine, nor any foul, stinking impurities.
Although he appears to consume food, nothing enters him; he does so solely out of compassion to benefit sentient beings, remaining free from all faults or afflictions in every circumstance.
He manifests the conduct of all ordinary worldlings, yet in reality he has no such conduct, having transcended all conditioned activities.
“Dṛḍhamati! When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is no difference between dwelling in a secluded place and dwelling in a village;
there is no difference between dwelling as a householder and dwelling as one who has left the household life.”
He appears as a layperson (*avadātavasana*) yet remains free from negligence;
he appears as a śramaṇa yet does not exalt himself.

Among the various paths of renunciation followed by non-Buddhists, he does not actually renounce anything for the sake of transforming sentient beings; he is untainted by any false views, nor does he claim to have attained purity therein.
He manifests all the rituals and practices of the non-Buddhists, yet does not follow the paths they travel. "Firm Mind!
It is like a guide who, having led a multitude of people across a perilous path, then leads others across as well."
Thus it is, Resolute Mind!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they follow the resolve for the Way awakened by sentient beings—whether it be the path of a śrāvaka, the path of a pratyekabuddha, or the awakening of the Buddha-path—and provide guidance according to what is appropriate so that they may attain liberation. Having done so, they immediately return to liberate other sentient beings; therefore, such a Great Being is called a "Guide."
It is like a sturdy ship that ferries immeasurable people from this shore to the other shore, and having reached the other shore, returns again to ferry others.
Thus it is, Resolute Mind!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they see all sentient beings fallen into the waters of birth and death, drifting upon the four currents. Desiring to deliver them and enable their liberation, [the bodhisattva] acts according to the maturation of the roots of goodness each has planted: if they see one who can be delivered by means of a pratyekabuddha, they immediately manifest their body to show the path to nirvāṇa;
if they see one who can be delivered by means of a śrāvaka, they preach the teaching of cessation for them so that they may enter nirvāṇa together.
"By the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he manifests rebirth once more to deliver and liberate other people; therefore, this Great Being is called a 'Captain.
O Resolute Mind!"
It is like a magician who, before a great multitude, manifests his own death—showing himself bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, or being consumed by fire, or devoured by birds and beasts.
Having manifested such a body before the crowd and having obtained wealth, he then rises up again, because he is well-versed in the art of illusion.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this way in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they manifest old age and death in order to transform sentient beings, yet in reality, there is no birth, aging, sickness, or death.
Resolute Mind!
"This is called the fundamental cause and retribution of the dhyāna-pāramitā of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:

"When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they cultivate wisdom and their faculties become sharp and keen; they have never perceived the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, yet for the sake of transformation, they speak of the existence of sentient beings."
Not perceiving a life-span or a living being, yet they speak of there being a life-span and a living being;
not attaining the nature of karma or the nature of karmic retribution, yet they demonstrate to sentient beings that there is karma and karmic retribution;
not attaining the nature of birth-and-death or the various afflictions, yet they say that one should know and see birth-and-death and the afflictions.
Without perceiving nirvana, they speak of reaching nirvana;
without perceiving any differentiated characteristics among all phenomena, they speak of phenomena being wholesome or unwholesome;
having already been able to cross over to the shore of unimpeded wisdom, they manifest birth in the desire realm yet remain unattached to the desire realm.
They manifest the practice of the dhyānas of the form realm yet do not cling to the form realm;
they manifest entry into the formless absorptions yet are born in the form realm;
they manifest the practice of the dhyānas of the form realm yet are born in the desire realm.
Though manifesting in the desire realm, they do not engage in the activities of the desire realm.

They fully know all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as well as their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*), and with mastery, they are able to enter and emerge from these absorptions at will. To transform sentient beings, they take birth according to their intentions, assuming physical form in every place of rebirth.

They are always able to accomplish profound and wondrous wisdom, severing all conditioned activities of sentient beings; yet, while manifesting engaged conduct for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they in reality perform no action toward any phenomena.
They have all already transcended all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have long since extinguished the mind of "I" and "mine," yet they manifest the acceptance of all necessary requisites.

When Bodhisattvas achieve such wisdom, whatever they do accords with that wisdom; they are never defiled by the fruits of karma. To transform sentient beings, they may manifest as mute, yet internally they truly possess the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice, having reached the further shore of linguistic expression and the scriptures.

Without first deliberating upon what Dharma he should preach, whatever he says to whichever assembly he encounters is sublime; he is able to gladden them all and cause their minds to become firm, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, yet the wisdom of this Bodhisattva does not diminish.

“Dṛḍhamati! It is like men or women, whether great or small, who take vessels with them and go to a body of water—be it a spring, a pond, a canal, a river, or the great ocean—and each returns with their vessel filled according to its size, yet these waters do not diminish at all.”
Thus it is, Resolute Mind!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, whatever assembly they enter—whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, śakras, or brahmās—they do not need to exert mental effort; they are able to gladden them all with virtuous words and expound the Dharma as is appropriate for each. Yet, their wisdom and eloquence do not diminish in the slightest.
“Dṛḍhamati! This is called the fruit of retribution for the fundamental practice of the Prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Buddha told Dṛḍhamati:

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all sentient beings who see him attain liberation and deliverance; some hear his name, some witness his dignified demeanor, some hear him preach the Dharma, and some see him in silence, yet all of them attain deliverance."
"Resolute Mind!
It is like the great king of medicinal trees named 'Joyful to Behold' (Priyadarśana); whoever sees it has all their illnesses cured.
In the same way, Resolute Mind!"
When Bodhisattvas abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all sentient beings who see them are cured of the diseases of greed, anger, and ignorance.

It is like a great medicinal king named "Eliminator": if it is used to coat drums during battle, those who have been pierced by arrows or wounded by swords and spears will find their arrows extracted and their poison removed upon hearing the sound of the drum.
Thus it is, Resolute Mind!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, those who hear its name will have the arrows of greed, anger, and delusion naturally extracted; all poisons of false views will be utterly extinguished, and no afflictions will ever again arise.
“Dṛḍhamati! It is like a medicinal tree named ‘Complete.

If someone uses its root, their illness is cured; its stem, nodes, heartwood, bark, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit can all cure illnesses. Whether it is fresh, dried, or cut into pieces, it can entirely cure the various diseases of sentient beings.”

It is the same for a bodhisattva dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi: there is no time when they do not benefit sentient beings, for they are always able to eliminate all their afflictions by means of preaching the Dharma while concurrently practicing the four methods of attraction and the various pāramitās, thereby enabling them to attain liberation.
Whether people offer them sustenance or not, whether it is beneficial or not, these bodhisattvas cause all beings to find peace and security through the benefits of the Dharma.

Even after their death, should there be those who eat their flesh—be they two-legged or four-legged animals, birds or beasts, humans or non-humans—all such sentient beings, by virtue of the power of the bodhisattva’s precepts and vows, shall be reborn in the heavens upon death, remaining forever free from illness, pain, decay, affliction, and all manner of suffering.
“Dṛḍhamati!
A bodhisattva who dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is like a medicinal tree.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Dṛḍhamati.

"When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they naturally know the six pāramitās in every lifetime without learning them from others; with every lifting and lowering of the foot, and with every inhalation and exhalation, the six pāramitās are ever present in every thought-moment."
Why is this? Resolute Mind!
Thus, the bodies of such bodhisattvas are entirely the Dharma, and their practices are entirely the Dharma.
Dṛḍhamati! It is like a king or his ministers who have ground together hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense into a powder.
Suppose someone were to come and ask for one specific kind from among them, not wishing for it to be mixed with or permeated by the other fragrances.
“Dṛḍhamati! Within these hundreds of thousands of varieties of powdered incense, could one find even a single kind that is not mixed with the others? “No, World-Honored One!”
“Dṛḍhamati! Because this bodhisattva has perfumed his body and mind with all the pāramitās, he constantly gives rise to the six pāramitās in every thought-moment.”
Dṛḍhamati! How does a bodhisattva give birth to the six pāramitās in every moment of thought? Dṛḍhamati!
That this bodhisattva relinquishes everything entirely with a mind free from greedy attachment is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā);
that the mind is well-quiescent and ultimately free from evil is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
and that knowing the nature of the exhaustion of the mind, one remains unharmed amidst all sensory objects is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Diligently observing and discerning the mind so that one knows the mind is free from signs is the *vīryapāramitā*;
bringing the mind to ultimate tranquility and subduing it is the *dhyānapāramitā*;
observing the mind and knowing the mind so as to penetrate the characteristics of the mind is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Dṛḍhamati! When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, such Dharma-gates as these are present in every thought-moment, each containing the six pāramitās.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
That which is practiced by a bodhisattva who has accomplished the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is inconceivable.”
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas wish to practice the conduct of a Buddha, they should study this Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Why is this so?”
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva manifests all the practices of ordinary worldlings, yet within his mind there is no greed, hatred, or delusion.
At that time, in the assembly, there was a Great Brahma King named Suvatsa who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva wishes to practice all the practices of ordinary worldlings, they should study the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Why is this?
"This bodhisattva manifests all the practices of ordinary worldlings, yet his mind is free from the activities of greed, hatred,
and delusion. The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
Excellent! Succeeding in Compassion!
It is just as you have said.
"If a bodhisattva wishes to practice all the practices of ordinary worldlings, they should study the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, because they do not dwell upon anything that is learned.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva wishes to study the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, how should they study it?
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:
“It is like learning archery: first, one shoots at a large target.”
Once one has mastered shooting at the large target, one learns to shoot at the small target;
once one has mastered shooting at the small target, one next learns to shoot at the bullseye;
having learned to shoot at the bullseye, one next learns to shoot at the staff.
Having mastered shooting at the staff, one learns to shoot at a bundle of a hundred hairs;
having mastered shooting at a hundred hairs, one learns to shoot at a bundle of ten hairs;
having mastered shooting at ten hairs, one learns to shoot at a single hair.
Having mastered shooting at a single hair, one trains to shoot at one-hundredth of a hair;
once capable of shooting this, one is called a skilled archer, whose arrows never miss at will.
If such a person, in the darkness of night, wishes to shoot at sounds heard—whether from humans or non-humans—they can do so without exerting mental effort, and every arrow will strike its mark.

Thus it is, Resolute Mind! A bodhisattva who wishes to study the Śūraṅgama Samādhi should first study the mind of loving joy; having studied the mind of loving joy, they should study the profound mind; having studied the profound mind, they should study great kindness; having studied great kindness, they should study great compassion; and having studied great compassion, they should study the four noble brahma-vihāras, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Having trained in the four noble Brahma-conducts, one should train in obtaining the five supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that naturally accompany the body; having trained in these powers, one is then able to accomplish the six *pāramitās*;
having accomplished the six *pāramitās*, one is then able to master skillful means (*upāya*);
and having mastered skillful means, one attains the third stage of patience, the Patience of Accordance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
Having dwelled in the third stage of compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the Buddhas bestow a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*);
and having received the prophecy from the Buddhas, one is able to enter the eighth bodhisattva stage.
Having entered the eighth bodhisattva stage, one attains the samādhi of the manifest presence of all buddhas;
having attained the samādhi of the manifest presence of all buddhas, one is never separated from seeing the buddhas;
being never separated from seeing the buddhas, one is able to fulfill the causes and conditions for all buddha-dharmas.
Having fulfilled all the causes and conditions for the Buddha-dharmas, one is able to give rise to the merit of adorning the Buddha-fields;
having given rise to the merit of adorning the Buddha-fields, one is able to possess a noble birth and lineage;
having possessed a noble birth and lineage, one enters the womb and is born.
Having entered the womb and been born, they are able to fulfill the ten stages;
having fulfilled the ten stages, they then receive the title and office of a Buddha;
having received the title and office of a Buddha, they then attain all the samādhis of the bodhisattvas.
Having attained all bodhisattva samādhis, one subsequently attains the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
having attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one is able to perform buddha-deeds for the sake of sentient beings, yet without abandoning the practices of a bodhisattva.
“Dṛḍhamati! If a bodhisattva studies these dharmas in this way, they will attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Once a bodhisattva has attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is nothing further among all dharmas for them to study.”
Why is this? Because they have already thoroughly mastered all dharmas.
It is like one who has studied archery and is able to hit a single hair’s breadth; they no longer need to study anything else.
Why is this? Because they have already trained previously.
Thus it is, Resolute Mind!
When a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is nothing further to be learned regarding any phenomena, for they have already mastered all samādhis and all merits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to speak a parable; I only pray that you will grant me your permission to do so.”
The Buddha said, "Speak then. [He replied,] "World-Honored One!"
For example, the Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm can naturally and universally survey the entire trichiliocosm without exerting any effort.
In this way, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are naturally able to contemplate all phenomena without exerting effort;
furthermore, they are also able to know the mental activities of every sentient being.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind: "It is as you have said.
If a bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they fully know all the dharmas of all bodhisattvas and all the buddha-dharmas."
At that time, there was Śakra, Lord of the Devas, named Sumerumūrdha, who dwelt at the very edge of this trichiliocosm; he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Just as one standing on the summit of Mount Sumeru can see everything throughout the world,
so too the bodhisattva, dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, is naturally able to observe the practices of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati asked the Śakra who held the summit of Mount Sumeru, saying:
"From which of the four continents have you come?
On which summit of Mount Sumeru do you dwell?"
The Śakra replied: "Good son!
If there is a bodhisattva who has attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one should not inquire as to his place of dwelling."
Why is this? For such a bodhisattva, all buddha-fields are dwelling places; yet they do not cling to dwelling places, do not apprehend dwelling places, and do not perceive dwelling places.
Dṛḍhamati asked, “Virtuous one,
have you attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
The Śākya replied:
“Within this samādhi, could there still be any marks of attainment or non-attainment?
Resolute Mind replied, “No.”
Śāriputra said:
"Good son! You should know that when a bodhisattva practices this samādhi, they attain nothing at all regarding any phenomena."
Dṛḍhamati said, "If your eloquence is such as this, you must have already attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The [other] one replied:
“Good son! I do not see any dharma that has a place of abiding; it is by not abiding in any dharma whatsoever that one attains the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.”
"Good son! Abiding in this samādhi, one abides in nothing at all regarding all phenomena; if there is no abiding, there is nothing to grasp;
if there is nothing to grasp, there is nothing to speak."
At that time, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati:
"Do you see this Śakra who holds Mount Sumeru? "I have seen him."
“World-Honored One!

“Firm Mind! This Śakra acts according to his own will; he is able to attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and by abiding in this samādhi, he can manifest his body in all the palaces of the Śakras throughout this trichiliocosm.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra of this world addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Śakra of Mount Sumeru is able to manifest his body within the palaces of the Śakras, why is it that I do not see him in any of the abodes of the Indras?”
At that time, Śakra who holds Mount Sumeru spoke to this Śakra, saying:
"Kauśika! If I were now to show you my true body, you would no longer find joy in your palace; yet I constantly go to the palace where you dwell, and you do not see me."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to behold this Great Being’s accomplishment of the wondrous body.”
The Buddha said,
"Kauśika! Do you wish to see it?"
“World-Honored One!
We wish most earnestly to see him.
The Buddha spoke to the Śakra who holds Mount Sumeru, saying:
“Good son! You must manifest this true and wondrous body of a Śakra.
Thereupon, that Śakra manifested his true and wondrous body.

At that time, among those in the assembly—the Śakras, Brahmās, World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas—who had not attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, their bodies all failed to appear, appearing like a mass of ink.
When Śakra, holding Mount Sumeru, became like the King of Mountains—lofty, towering, and with radiance shining afar—the Buddha’s body became twice as manifest.
Śakra Devānām-Indra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!

Now, the physical form and color of this Great Being are pure, exquisite, and beyond compare; the bodies of all these Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Heavenly Kings do not appear before him, appearing like a mass of ink.
“World-Honored One!
While I was upon the Sublime Hall of Mount Sumeru, wearing a necklace of Śakrābhilagna-maṇi jewels, by the radiance of these jewels, the bodies of all the celestial hosts became invisible.”
"Now, because of this Great Being’s radiance, my body no longer appears, and even the precious necklaces I wear have lost their luster.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra, "Kauśika!..."
If this trichiliocosm were filled with Śākyavimalagarbha maṇi jewels, and there were further illuminating celestial maṇi jewels that could cause these jewels to no longer appear at all.

Kauśika! Suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with the illuminating maṇi-jewels of the various devas; yet there is another, the Vajra-light maṇi-jewel, which can cause all those other jewels to no longer appear.
Kauśika! Suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with *vajraprabhā-maṇi* jewels, and there were further *sarvavidyāsaṃgraha-maṇi* jewels that could cause all those former jewels to no longer appear.
“Kauśika! Do you see this Maṇiratna-samuccaya jewel worn by Śakra? “I have seen it.”
“World-Honored One!
It is only because the radiance of this jewel is so fierce and intense that my eyes cannot endure it.
The Buddha told Kauśika:
"If there are bodhisattvas who have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi or who act as Śakra, they all wear such maṇi necklaces.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Those beings who do not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall not obtain such a pure and wondrous body, and they will likewise lose this Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Then the devaputra Gopaka said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"As for the śrāvakas who have already entered the stage of certainty (dharmatāniyāma), even if they were to praise and delight in the Buddha-way, they would be unable to achieve it, for they have already established a barrier between themselves and saṃsāra."

If a person has already resolved their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or is resolving it now, or will resolve it in the future, that person should love and delight in the Buddha-way, for they will be able to attain such a supreme and wondrous physical body.
For example, suppose there is a person who has been blind from birth; although they may praise and cherish the sun and moon, they do not receive their light.
In the same way, those śrāvakas who have entered the stage of the Dharma (dharmapada), though they may praise and cherish the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha’s merits bring no benefit to their bodies.
Therefore, if one wishes to attain this wondrous body of great wisdom, one should resolve to attain the unsurpassed Bodhicitta of a Buddha; thereby, one will obtain such a sublime physical form.
When the devaputra Gopaka spoke these words, twelve thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati asked the devaputra Gopaka:
"By practicing what merit does one transform the female body?"
He replied: "Good son!
Those who have set out in the Mahāyāna do not perceive the distinction between male and female."
Why is this so? Because the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) does not abide within the three realms; it is because of conceptual discrimination that there are men and women.
Regarding what you have asked, "By practicing what merit does one transform the female body? [the answer is as follows:]
"In the past, when serving the Bodhisattva, my mind was free from flattery and crookedness.
[The King asked: "In what manner did you serve him? He replied:
“As you have said, World-Honored One!
How is it that his mind is not crooked or deceitful? He replied:
“Physical action follows speech, and verbal action follows intention; this is called a woman’s mind being free from flattery and crookedness. She asked:
“How does one transform the female body?”
He replied, “It is as if it were accomplished. He asked:
"How is it as it is accomplished? He replied,
"It is like a turning."
He asked, "Devaputra, what is the meaning of these words? He replied:
“Good son! Among all dharmas, there is neither accomplishment nor turning; all dharmas have a single flavor, namely, the flavor of the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Good son!”
"According to my vow, I have this female body; even if my body were to become that of a man, I would not destroy or abandon the characteristics of a woman’s body. Good son!"
Therefore, you should know that both "male" and "female" are equally inverted; all dharmas and these inversions are ultimately devoid of dual characteristics.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati asked Gopaka:
"Do you know even a small portion of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi? He replied:
“Good son! I know that others have attained it, yet I have not personally realized it myself.
I recall that in a past life, when Śākyamuni Buddha was a bodhisattva in the household of King Śuddhodana, he was dwelling within the palace amidst a multitude of court ladies at midnight in purity.”

At that time, Brahma kings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges from the eastern direction arrived; some inquired about the Bodhisattva vehicle, while others inquired about the path of the Śrāvaka, and the Bodhisattvas each answered according to their respective questions.
Among the assembly of Brahmās, there was a Brahmā King who, not understanding the skillful means practiced by the Bodhisattva, spoke these words:
"Virtuous one, you possess such wisdom as to answer questions so well; why then do you crave the throne and sensual desires?"
The other Brahma kings, having fully understood the bodhisattva’s wisdom and skillful means, said to this Brahma:

"The bodhisattva does not crave royal rank or sensual desires; rather, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings to bring them to maturity, he dwells in the household life manifesting as a bodhisattva, while now elsewhere he has perfected the Buddha-way and is turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma."
Having heard this, that Brahmā spoke these words:
"What samādhi has been attained that enables such sovereign supernormal transformations?
The other Brahmās replied:
"This is the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Good son! At that time, I had this thought:

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in samādhi, his spiritual power and resonance reach the level of the unprecedented; though he remains amidst sensual desires and manages the affairs of state, he is nonetheless able not to depart from such samādhi."

Having heard this, my reverence redoubled; I conceived the thought of the World-Honored One toward the Bodhisattva, deeply resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and vowed that in a future life I too shall accomplish such merit as this.
"Good son! What I have seen is but a small portion; I know only this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, which shall possess immeasurable and inconceivable power and merit."
Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
That this Devaputra Gopaka has spoken thus from the depths of his heart is entirely because the Tathāgata has acted as his spiritual friend and constantly protected him.”
“World-Honored One!
Before long, the devaputra Gopaka shall also abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and attain such power of sovereign spiritual transformations, no different from what the World-Honored One now performs.”
The Bodhisattva Resolute Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there anyone present in this assembly who has attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi?”
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Abhimāna who said to the bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati:
"Suppose a merchant enters the great ocean and says:
'Is it possible to take with me the maṇi-jewel that is in this great ocean?'"
"Your words seem appropriate. Why is this?

Within this present great ocean-like assembly of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, there are bodhisattvas who have accomplished the treasure of the Dharma and have donned the great armor of adornment; you sit among them and ask such a question."
“Is there, within this assembly, any bodhisattva who has attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi? “Dṛḍhamati!

Within this very assembly, there are bodhisattvas who have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and manifest the body of Śakra; some manifest the body of Brahmā; and some manifest the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.”
There are those who, having attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, manifest the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
there are those who, having attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, adorn their own bodies with the various marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*);

and among the bodhisattvas themselves, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, there are those who manifest the physical form, color, and appearance of women, those who manifest the physical form and appearance of śrāvakas, and those who manifest the physical form and appearance of pratyekabuddhas.

Dṛḍhamati! Just as the Tathāgata, by his sovereign power, manifests throughout whatever assemblies he enters—whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, Śakras, Brahmās, or the world-protectors—he is able to universally manifest forms, colors, and physical characteristics within these various assemblies; you should know that all of this is the fruit of retribution resulting from the fundamental practices of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

Dṛḍhamati! If you see a place where the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma, you should know that therein there are immeasurable great bodhisattvas who possess mastery over great wisdom, who have donned the great armor, who act with mastery over all dharmas, and who are able to turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now maintain that this Devaputra Abhimānī has attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, for his wisdom, unimpeded eloquence, and supernormal powers are such as these.”
The Buddha said, “Dṛḍhamati! It is as you have said.
This Devaputra Abhimānī has already dwelled in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; because he has attained mastery of this samādhi, he is able to speak thus.”
At that time, the Buddha said to the Devaputra Abhimānacintin,
"You may now manifest a small portion of the original events of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Devaputra Abhimānacintin then spoke to Dṛḍhamati:
“O Benevolent One!
Would you like to see the limited power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi? He replied:
“Devaputra! I wish most earnestly to see it.

Because the Devaputra Abhimānī had well attained the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he immediately manifested a miraculous transformation, causing all those in the assembly to become universal monarchs (cakravartin), adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, accompanied by their retinues and the seven treasures.
The Devaputra asked,
"What do you see? Dṛḍhamati replied:
"I see that all those in the assembly have become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), with their physical marks, retinues, and the seven treasures as attendants.

At that time, the devaputra again manifested the assembly such that they all became Śakra-devānām-indra, dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa palace, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens performing various musical performances for their entertainment;

furthermore, by his supernormal power, he caused the entire assembly to universally assume the physical marks and majestic deportment of Brahmā kings, dwelling in the Brahma palace and practicing the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
He asked Dṛḍhamati again, "What do you see? He replied:
“Devaputra! I see that this entire assembly consists solely of Brahma kings.

He then manifested his supernatural power, causing the entire assembly to universally assume the physical form and appearance of the Elder Mahākāśyapa; holding their robes and bowls, they entered various meditative absorptions and practiced the eight liberations, all without any difference.

He further manifested his supernatural powers, causing the entire assembly to universally assume the physical marks, secondary characteristics, and dignified deportment of Śākyamuni Buddha, each surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus.
He asked again:
"Dṛḍhamati! What do you see?"
He replied, “Devaputra!
I see that this great assembly consists entirely of the physical forms, marks of excellence, and majestic deportment of Śākyamuni Buddha, each surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus.”
The Devaputra Abhimānacitta said to Sthāmamati:
"Such is the sovereign power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi! Sthāmamati!"

When a bodhisattva attains the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are able to place a trichiliocosm within a mustard seed, yet cause all its mountains, rivers, suns, moons, and stars to appear exactly as they were before, without any crowding, manifesting this to all sentient beings.
“Dṛḍhamati! The inconceivable power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is thus!
At that time, the great disciples, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting kings, spoke to the Buddha with one voice, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a person attains this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, that person’s merit is inconceivable. Why is this so?
Such a person has reached the ultimate path of the Buddha, having accomplished wisdom, supernormal powers, and the various illuminations.
Today, while seated upon a single seat, we have universally beheld the manifold forms and various manifestations of this assembly; we reflect thus:
"If a person does not hear the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one should know that this provides an opportunity for Māra to gain the upper hand."
"If one should hear this, it should be known that such a person is protected by all Buddhas; how much more so for one who, having heard it, practices according to what they have taught!
"World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva wishes to penetrate the Buddha-dharma and reach the other shore, they should listen with a single mind to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and explain it to others."
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva wishes to universally manifest all forms, colors, and modes of conduct; wishes to fully and universally know the mental activities and thoughts of all sentient beings; and further wishes to universally know how to provide medicine according to the illness of all sentient beings, they should attentively listen to this Dharma-treasure of samādhi and receive, uphold, read, and recite it.”
“World-Honored One!
If a person attains this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one should know that this person has entered the realm of the Buddha and possesses mastery over wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

If a person does not attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they cannot be called a Bodhisattva of profound practice; the Tathāgata would not say that such a person is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore, if you wish to travel all paths, you should study to attain this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, because it involves not dwelling on anything that is learned.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind asked the Devaputra Manifest Mind:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain this samādhi, what dharmas should they practice?"
The devaputra replied:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain this samādhi, they should practice the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one perceives that the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the Buddha are neither conjoined nor dispersed, this is called the cultivation and accumulation of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."
Dṛḍhamati asked, "In the Buddha-dharma, is there any joining together or dispersing?
The devaputra replied:
“In the dharmas of ordinary beings, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion; how much less so in the Buddha-dharmas?
“What is called ‘cultivation’?
“If one can penetrate the fact that the dharmas of ordinary beings and the Buddha-dharmas are non-dual, this is called ‘cultivated accumulation.’”
Yet in reality, this dharma is without conjunction and without dispersion. Good son!
All dharmas are gathered because they lack the characteristic of arising.
The collection of all dharmas is because they possess no characteristic of disintegration;
the collection of all dharmas is because they possess the characteristic of space;
the collection of all dharmas is because they possess no characteristic of sensation.
Dṛḍhamati asked again:
“To what place does the Śūraṅgama-samādhi go?
The devaputra replied:
"The Śūraṅgama Samādhi reaches into the mental activities of all sentient beings, yet it does not grasp at signs by taking those mental activities as objects;
it reaches into all places of birth, yet it is not defiled by those places of birth;
it reaches to the presence of the Buddhas in all worlds, yet it does not differentiate the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body."
They reach all sounds and languages, yet do not discriminate among the characteristics of written characters;
they are able to universally reveal all Buddha-dharmas, yet do not arrive at a point of ultimate exhaustion.
"Good son! As for your question regarding where this samādhi reaches:
wherever the Buddha goes, this samādhi likewise reaches."
Dṛḍhamati asked, "To where has the Buddha gone?
The devaputra replied:
"Because the Buddha is suchness (tathatā), he reaches that which is nowhere to be reached.
He asked again:
"Does the Buddha not reach nirvana?"
He replied: "All dharmas are ultimately nirvana; therefore, the Tathāgata does not go to nirvana. Why is this? Because..."
"Because it has the nature of nirvāṇa, it does not reach nirvāṇa.
He asked again:
"Did the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not reach nirvāṇa?"
He replied, "Are the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges born from this? Dṛḍhamati said:
“The Tathāgata has said that the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having been born, have entered parinirvāṇa.
The Devaputra said:
“O Son of Good Family!...”
The Tathāgata does not say that one person appearing in the world brings great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings.
What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata definitively hold that all sentient beings undergo birth and cessation?
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
The Tathāgata does not perceive arising or ceasing within the dharmas."
“Good son! You should know that although the Tathāgata speaks of all Buddhas appearing in the world, in the mark of the Tathāgata there is in fact no birth;
although he speaks of all Buddhas attaining nirvana, in the mark of the Tathāgata there is in fact no extinction.”
He asked again:
"Are there currently immeasurable Tathāgatas who have attained the Way? He replied:
“The Tathāgata’s realization of the Way is such that it is characterized by neither arising nor ceasing.
O son of good family!
Whether the Buddhas appear in the world or enter parinirvāṇa, there is no distinction between them.”
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has realized that all phenomena possess the characteristic of quiescence; this is what is called a Buddha.
He asked again:
"If all phenomena are ultimately quiescent and possess the characteristic of nirvāṇa, can their characteristic of penetration be realized? He replied,
"Just as all phenomena are ultimately quiescent and identical to the characteristic of nirvāṇa, so too is the characteristic of penetration."
“Good son! The Tathāgata does not appear through birth, abiding, or cessation; that which is without birth, abiding, or cessation is called the appearance of a Buddha. Jianyi asked:
“Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, are you able to speak in such a manner? He replied, “Good son!
"What do you think?
Within what dharma does a person created by the Tathāgata abide when they speak?
Dhṛtiprāpta replied:
"Relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, one is able to speak.
He asked again:
"In what place does the Buddha abide when he creates a manifested person?"
He replied, "The Buddha dwells in non-dual supernormal power and creates emanated beings.
The devaputra said:
"Just as the Tathāgata, abiding in the dharma of non-abiding, manifests emanated beings, so too do those emanated beings, abiding in the dharma of non-abiding, have something to say.
Resolute Mind said: "If there is no abiding, how can there be speech?"
The devaputra said: "Just as there is no abiding, so too is the teaching.
He asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva fulfill the eloquence of joyful speech? He replied:
“When a bodhisattva speaks without the mark of a self, without the mark of another, and without the mark of phenomena, this is called fulfilling the eloquence of joyful speech.”
In accordance with the Dharma taught, the characteristics of words and letters are inexhaustible, and the characteristics of phenomena are likewise inexhaustible.
One who speaks in this manner does not speak dualistically; this is called the perfection of the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
Furthermore, noble son!

If a bodhisattva does not abandon the illusory characteristics of all phenomena, and does not abandon the echo-like characteristics of all sounds, this is called being fully endowed with the eloquence of joyful speech.

Furthermore, just as all letters, sounds, and languages have no location, no direction, no interior, and no exterior, and do not abide anywhere, but exist through a multitude of conditions; so it is with this.

All dharmas are likewise thus: they have no location, no direction, no interior, and no exterior; they abide nowhere, are neither past, future, nor present, and cannot be expressed by letters or words. To internally realize this for oneself and yet speak of it—this is called the eloquence of complete and joyful exposition.
"It is like an echo; all sounds are spoken in accordance with the characteristics of an echo.
Jianyi asked, "In what sense does 'in accordance' mean this?"
“Good son! To follow space is to follow the meaning.
Just as space has nothing to follow, so too all teachings have nothing to follow.”
"All dharmas are peerless and beyond analogy; for those who have attained them, it is said that there is something to follow.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the devaputra, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent! It is as you have said.
A bodhisattva should not be terrified by this.
"Why is this? If there is anything to follow after, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From which buddha-field has this Devaputra Manifest Mind come to this place?
The devaputra replied:
“Question: ‘What are you doing? Resolute Mind replied:
‘I now wish to pay homage toward that direction, for it is the place where this Great Being dwells and wanders.’”
The devaputra said to him:
"If anyone should obtain this Śūraṅgama Samādhi with their own hands, all the gods and people of the world should pay them homage and respect."
